title: Withdrawals decrement the rate limit by the decoded realized amount, not by the amount requested
content:
The withdraw process ends with two coupled steps. First the operator "must decode the raw bytes data returned from the `doCall()` function into `uint256` value, representing the amount of underlying assets that were successfully withdrawn from the Aave pool (`amountWithdrawn`)" (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.2.1.3.2.6.3). Then "the operator must decrease the `RateLimit` based on the assets redeemed" (.3.2.7), shown as `rateLimits.triggerRateLimitDecrease(RateLimitHelpers.makeAssetKey(LIMIT_AAVE_WITHDRAW, aToken), amountWithdrawn)`.

The accounting is deliberately settled against reality rather than intent. Aave withdrawals can return less than requested — capped by available pool liquidity or by the balance actually held — and if the limit were decremented by the requested `amount`, capacity would be consumed for value that never moved. Over repeated partial fills a purely intent-based accounting would silently starve the conduit.

This produces an ordering the runbook makes explicit: the rate limit is *checked* before the call (.3.2.3, using the same `LIMIT_AAVE_WITHDRAW` key) but *decremented* after it, using post-execution data. Check-then-reconcile, not check-and-reserve.

The residual risk is the gap between the two: between the pre-check and the decrease, the recorded remaining capacity overstates what is truly available. In a single atomic transaction that window is closed, which is precisely why the decode and the decrease are specified as steps of the same function rather than as a follow-up operation.
description: The withdraw path decodes amountWithdrawn from the return data and calls triggerRateLimitDecrease with that value, so partial fills consume only the capacity they actually used.
